stops.name: Cerro Rico de Potosí, the summit
stops.campa: The mountain stands perfect as a bell over the highest city of the world, red in the morning, violet at dusk, hollowed within like a honeycomb of silver. Beneath it swarm one hundred and sixty thousand souls, more than Seville, more than London; fourteen nations of Spain quarrel in its streets and kill each other like barbarians. Kings say 'vale un Potosí' when they mean a thing beyond price. And the mountain waits, patient, for the two girls it is about to make; one day it will rise again, sun-crowned, on the first coin and the shield of a republic not yet born, Belgrano's Potosí.

stops.name: Bocamina on the Cerro, the mouths of the mita
stops.campa: At the mine mouths the mitayos go down by tallow-light, ladders of hide dropping into warm darkness, and come up bent under the ore that will be coined into half the money of the earth. The Villa below spends what the mountain vomits: eight fencing schools where men learn the manner of killing one another, fourteen schools of dance attended by men and women alike, gaming houses, comedias, bulls. The chronicle calls it the most splendid and the most quarrelsome town of the Indies. This is the city that eats men, and it is about to meet two doncellas it cannot eat.

stops.name: Munaypata, the two houses at the entrance of the barrio
stops.campa: At the entrance of Munaypata, where the road drops toward the ingenios of Cantumarca, stand two houses of neighbors. In one lives don Antonio de Souza, a noble Portuguese, with his son don Juan and a most beautiful little daughter, Eustaquia. In the other live don Pedro Urinza, an Andalusian knight, and his wife doña Plácida Lezama, whose only child, Ana, is a pilgrim wonder of beauty. Two girls born within a year of each other, under the same silver mountain, in the same dust of the same street. The chronicle sets down their names as if setting two blades side by side.

stops.name: Casa de don Antonio de Souza, the orphan comes to the house
stops.campa: Doña Plácida dies while Ana is still tender, and within two years don Pedro follows her, leaving the child in the power of don Antonio de Souza, to be raised there in the company of doña Eustaquia, who at that season is likewise four years old. So the orphan of the Andalusian crosses the street and never leaves. The two girls grow as one flesh; Ana calls don Antonio and his wife father and mother, having no others. In the city of fourteen quarreling nations, one household holds a Portuguese rose and an Andalusian ember, and does not yet know what it holds.

stops.name: The estrado of the Souza house: embroidery, dance and forbidden windows
stops.campa: The girls are raised in such seclusion that neither the town nor even the barrio knows such children exist. They hear mass in the oratory of the house and enter a church scarcely ten times a year. On the estrado they are set to the almohadillas, the little embroidery cushions, and to the dances proper to doncellas. But the house has a servant boy, and he tells them of the fiestas, the comedias, the bulls, the saraos and other rejoicings of the Villa, and every word, says the chronicle, only quickens their desire to go out and see it.

stops.name: Behind the door, don Juan at his fencing lesson
stops.campa: Don Antonio has his son don Juan taught to manage and play the arms of steel and of fire, and keeps weapons of every kind in the house. While the master's blade rings against the boy's, two faces watch from behind the door: Eustaquia and Ana take great pleasure in that divertimiento, and it grieves them, the chronicle says plainly, not to be men so as to wield those arms themselves. Every parry enters their eyes and is kept. The sword is learned first by stolen sight, the way saints first learn their visions: unasked, entire, and in secret.

stops.name: The jug of water: death of don Juan de Souza
stops.campa: Don Juan is fencing with his master, sweating with the exercise, and asks for a jug of water. He drinks it, and within twenty-four hours the water has killed him: fifteen years old, the pride of his father, undone not by any blade but by a cup. The house falls into mourning; the very instrument by which don Antonio sought his son's estimation in this life becomes the origin of his greatest sorrow. Eustaquia and Ana are thirteen. The chronicle marks the hinge exactly: from this death, all their deeds descend. The brother's sword lies masterless in the house of weapons.

stops.name: The secret salle: sword, dagger, harquebus, horse
stops.campa: Fifteen months after don Juan, his mother follows him to the grave, and the girls remain alone with don Antonio. Now, whenever the father goes out, the two doncellas amuse themselves learning to fire the weapons of fire and to play the weapons of steel, thirteen years old, with more inclination to grip arms than to take up the embroidery cushions. The tradition adds that the dead boy's master, persuaded and sworn, perfects in secret what stolen sight began: sword, dagger, harquebus, and the horse. In the city of eight fencing schools, the best salle has no sign and two pupils.

stops.name: The first sally, a street of Munaypata, and Diego Melgarejo
stops.campa: By night the doncellas become caballeros. Dressed as men, armed from their father's house, they slip past the sleeping door and stop a passing youth to be their guide; he leaves what he carries and returns swiftly with a cloak and a dagger at his belt. His name is Diego Melgarejo, and he will be the secretary of all their deeds. Grateful, they tell him the truth, uncovering beautiful laughing faces and speaking in sweetest voices. Two centuries before, a maid of Domrémy put on man's iron and was believed; the crossing of dress is Joan's, and Potosí receives it.

stops.name: Plazuela de San Lorenzo, first blood, against Pimentel's ronda
stops.campa: Melgarejo leads them down the principal streets without event, until, turning home, they meet in the plazuela de San Lorenzo the servants and blacks of the justicia mayor don Luis Pimentel, who go out at night in the guise of a ronda to commit a thousand insolences, squeezing craftsmen and Indians of their goods. Steel answers insolence: a criado of the justicia mayor is left dead on the stones. The valiant doncellas set hands to swords to pursue the rest, and only Melgarejo's terror drags them home. Next day president Nestares Marín and Pimentel turn the Villa over, and can discover nothing.

stops.name: The door at ten o'clock, víspera de San Juan
stops.campa: On Saint John's Eve at ten of the night Melgarejo waits at their door, praying to God they never come out, though he carries two pistolets now, thinking valor lives in such things. They come out. The chronicle dresses them piece by piece, armorer and lover at once: damascened cutlasses and strong bucklers, black hats, scarlet capes covered with points of silver, short skirts of silver cloth scarcely veiling the knee, doublets of blue brocade, and beneath, coats of mail. Into their guide's hands they give a most sweet vihuela, for singing in this or that street, as is the custom of the land.

stops.name: Plaza del Gato, the serenade
stops.campa: Having walked some streets they come to the plaza del Gato, the market square of the fourteen nations, and seat themselves upon the stone benches as if these were the estrados of their own house. The gracious Eustaquia tunes her instrument and sweetly sings whatever she pleases, and her delicate voice and skill draw to her much of the strolling night-people of the town. Two masked caballeros, mail under brocade, playing music in the murder-streets: the city that eats men gathers round to listen, and does not know it is being serenaded by its own daughters.
